rules.title: Prohibition on landlord application fees and other upfront charges
rules.quote: It states that prior to the beginning of a tenancy, no lessor may require payment for anything except first, last, security, and locks (MGL Ch 186 Section 15B).
rules.summary: Landlords may not charge application fees, pet fees, cleaning fees, amenity fees, or any other charges before a tenancy begins; only first month's rent, last month's rent, security deposit, and lock-change fees are allowed.
rules.key_value: First, last, security, and locks only
rules.coverage_text: Applies to all lessors in Massachusetts
rules.exemption_note: Licensed brokers may charge application fees under 254 CMR 7, but landlords (even if also licensed brokers) may not.
rules.penalty: Perry v Equity Residential Management, LLC (2014) federal district court case awarded tenants treble damages and attorney's fees for unlawful application fees.

rules.title: Licensed broker application fee authorization and requirements
rules.quote: The board's regulations set out certain detailed requirements, including the steps that a licensed broker must take when dealing with prospective tenants (254 C.M.R. 7).
rules.summary: Licensed brokers (not landlords) may charge application fees to prospective tenants if they comply with board of registration regulations, including providing written notice of the fee amount, payment terms, and contingency at the first personal meeting.
rules.coverage_text: Applies only to licensed brokers helping connect property owners with prospective tenants
rules.exemption_note: Broker must hold a valid license. In Samia v. McElaney (1983), Housing Court held broker fee allowed only if 'separate bona fide business operation' and not simply landlord wearing different hat.
rules.penalty: Woodruff v. Niles Co., Inc. (2007) allowed class action against management company that hired broker whose license had expired.
